name: English Language
areas: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities

points.title: The role of Standard English in informal texts
points.detail: How SAE functions as the reference point that informality is measured against, and what it means for a text to depart from it deliberately rather than through error.

questions.q: Explain why a text can depart from Standard English deliberately rather than through error, and describe how you would tell the two apart in an informal text.
answer: Standard English is the codified variety used as a reference point, not a measure of correctness.
Deliberate departure is systematic and serves a purpose — solidarity, identity, humour, speed.
Error is inconsistent and serves no communicative function.
Consistency across the text, and whether the feature fits the tenor and audience, distinguish them.

points.title: Functions of language in a given context
points.detail: Jakobson's six functions — referential, emotive, conative, phatic, metalinguistic, poetic — and identifying which are operating in a text, usually more than one.

questions.q: A friend texts: 'hey u free sat? think im gonna lose it if i dont get out of the house lol'. Identify two functions of language operating and justify each.
answer: Referential — the message conveys information and a question about Saturday availability.
Emotive — 'lose it', 'lol' express the speaker's emotional state.
Also acceptable: phatic, maintaining the social connection between friends.
Conative if the request is read as directing the friend to respond.

points.title: Register, tenor and audience in informal texts
points.detail: How the relationship between participants, their social distance and the assumed audience drive the level of informality.

questions.q: Explain how tenor shapes the level of informality, using the contrast between a message to a sibling and one to a new employer.
answer: Tenor is the relationship between participants, including social distance and relative power.
Low social distance and equal power with a sibling permit slang, ellipsis and minimal mitigation.
High social distance and unequal power with an employer require standard forms, full clauses and negative politeness.
The same speaker shifts register because the tenor changes, not their ability.

points.title: Features of informal writing
points.detail: Across a range of texts: abbreviations, spellings reflecting pronunciation, syntactic creativity, ellipsis, shortened lexical forms, non-linear structure.

questions.q: Identify four features that mark a written text as informal and explain what each contributes to the relationship between writer and reader.
answer: Contractions and shortenings — signal casualness and speed.
Colloquial lexis or slang — signals shared identity and reduces social distance.
Ellipsis and sentence fragments — assume shared context between writer and reader.
Non-standard orthography, emojis, lower case — substitute for prosody and mark intimacy.
Each should be tied to intimacy, solidarity or equality.

card.title: Features of informal writing
card.front: What marks a written text as informal?
back: Lexis — colloquialism, slang, contractions, shortenings, hypocoristics
Syntax — ellipsis, sentence fragments, coordination over subordination
Orthography — non-standard spelling, lower case, repeated letters
Emojis and graphemes substituting for prosody
Discourse — loose structure, first and second person, direct address

points.title: Features of informal speech
points.detail: Spontaneity and planning both playing a role, prosodic and paralinguistic support, and the idiosyncratic choices individual speakers make.

questions.q: Explain why non-fluency features in a transcript are evidence of informality rather than evidence of a poor speaker.
answer: Spontaneous speech is planned in real time, so pauses, false starts and repairs are expected.
Their presence shows low planning and an unrehearsed exchange, characteristic of informal contexts.
Filled pauses also hold the floor while the speaker formulates the next utterance.
Judging them as errors is a prescriptivist reading; descriptively they are normal features of speech.

card.title: Features of informal speech
card.front: What marks a spoken text as informal?
back: Non-fluency: filled pauses, false starts, repetition, repairs
Connected speech processes throughout
Overlapping speech, backchannels, latching
Colloquial and slang lexis, swearing, taboo
Simple syntax, ellipsis, high context-dependence
Spontaneity — but planning still appears in places

points.title: Context and language features in informal texts
points.detail: The relationship between the situational and cultural context of an exchange and the specific features that appear in it — the heart of every analytical commentary.

questions.q: Explain how the situational context of a group chat between close friends produces the specific language features found in it.
answer: Tenor: close, equal relationships mean low social distance and minimal face mitigation.
Field: everyday personal subject matter allows colloquial lexis rather than specialised terms.
Mode: written but spontaneous, so it borrows spoken features — ellipsis, fragments, emojis for prosody.
Shared cultural context means much can be left implicit, producing high inference and in-group references.

card.title: How context shapes features
card.front: Link situational context to the features that appear — informal and formal.
back: Field — the subject matter drives the lexis and any jargon
Tenor — relationship and social distance set the politeness and formality
Mode — spoken or written changes planning, cohesion and non-fluency
Setting — public or private, immediate or distant audience
Informal: shared context means more can be left implicit
Formal: context must be made explicit for an unknown audience

points.title: Features of spoken discourse in informal texts
points.detail: Openings and closings, adjacency pairs, minimal responses, overlapping speech, discourse markers and non-fluency features, and what each contributes.

questions.q: Explain how openings and closings differ between an informal conversation between friends and a formal job interview.
answer: Informal: openings are loose, may skip greetings entirely, and closings are negotiated over several turns.
Formal: openings follow convention with explicit greetings and often self-identification.
Formal closings are managed by the participant with higher status, signalling the end clearly.
The difference reflects tenor — social distance requires more explicit structuring.

card.title: Spoken discourse in informal and formal texts
card.front: Which discourse features appear, and which get suppressed, in each?
back: Informal — openings/closings loose, overlap common, non-fluency frequent
Informal — adjacency pairs casual, backchannels constant
Formal — turns allocated by role, overlap rare, non-fluency edited out
Formal — planned openings and closings, explicit topic management
Formal speech carries written-language organisation with spoken delivery

points.title: Subsystem patterning, colloquial language and slang
points.detail: Identifying patterning across the subsystems, and the role of colloquialisms and slang in marking informality and in-group membership.

questions.q: Distinguish colloquial language from slang, and explain how each contributes to informality in a text between teenagers.
answer: Colloquial language is informal but widely understood across the speech community.
Slang is group-specific, changes faster, and marks membership of a particular group.
Colloquialism lowers formality and signals a relaxed register.
Slang additionally excludes outsiders and constructs in-group identity for the participants.

points.title: Taboo language, dysphemism and swearing
points.detail: Swearing patterns and taboo language as markers of informality and solidarity, and the social work they do beyond giving offence.

questions.q: A transcript of close friends contains repeated swearing. Explain why this is not necessarily aggressive, and identify what it is likely achieving.
answer: Swearing is not only used to offend — its function depends on context and tenor.
Among close friends it commonly signals solidarity and in-group membership.
It marks the exchange as informal and relaxed, where taboo constraints can be suspended.
It can also intensify emotion or add humour rather than express hostility.

points.title: Emoticons, emojis and context-specific graphemes
points.detail: How written informal texts substitute for prosody and paralinguistics, and how a grapheme's meaning shifts with context.

questions.q: Explain how emojis and non-standard orthography compensate for the absence of prosodic and paralinguistic features in written informal texts.
answer: Written text lacks pitch, stress, volume and facial expression, which carry attitude in speech.
Emojis substitute for facial expression, marking humour, sarcasm or softening a face-threatening act.
Capitals and repeated letters substitute for volume and elongation ('STOP', 'nooooo').
Meaning is context-specific and varies between groups and generations.

card.title: Emojis, graphemes and multi-word lexemes
card.front: How do written informal texts replace prosody, and what is a multi-word lexeme?
back: Emojis and emoticons substitute for facial expression and tone
Meaning is context-specific and shifts between groups and generations
Capitals, repeated letters and punctuation stand in for volume and pitch
Context-specific graphemes — symbols meaningful only in their setting
Multi-word lexeme — stored and retrieved as one unit (idioms, phrasal verbs)

points.title: Discourse strategies and cooperation
points.detail: Topic management, turn-taking, repair sequences, and the ways speakers cooperate to keep an interaction running.

questions.q: Using the concepts of turn-taking, topic management and repair, explain how participants in an informal conversation cooperate.
answer: Turn-taking: participants use prosodic and grammatical cues to pass the floor; overlap is often supportive.
Topic management: topics are introduced, developed and shifted collaboratively rather than controlled by one speaker.
Repair: self-repair and other-repair fix breakdowns without threatening face.
Backchannels signal continued attention, encouraging the speaker to continue.

card.title: Discourse strategies and cooperation
card.front: How do speakers cooperate to keep a conversation running?
back: Turn-taking — cues that pass the floor; overlap can support or compete
Topic management — initiating, shifting and closing topics
Repair sequences — self-repair and other-repair when it breaks down
Minimal responses and backchannels (mm, yeah) show active listening
Discourse markers (so, anyway, well) signal structure
Code switching signals shared group membership

points.title: Informality for intimacy, solidarity and equality
points.detail: How informal choices reduce social distance, including the politeness strategies that support it.

questions.q: Explain how informal language can be used to build solidarity, and identify two specific features that achieve this.
answer: Solidarity is the sense of shared identity and belonging between participants.
Feature: slang or in-group lexis, comprehensible only to members, marking who belongs.
Feature: hypocoristics and nicknames, signalling familiarity and reducing social distance.
Also acceptable: swearing used non-aggressively, ellipsis assuming shared knowledge, positive politeness.

card.title: Why speakers choose informality
card.front: Informal language for intimacy, solidarity and equality — how does each work?
back: Intimacy — cuts social distance: nicknames, hypocoristics, in-jokes
Solidarity — signals shared identity: slang, swearing, ellipsis
Equality — flattens hierarchy: first names, colloquialism, positive politeness
Also: linguistic innovation, negotiating taboo, building rapport
In an analysis, always tie the specific feature to the purpose

points.title: Informality for innovation, harmony and in-group membership
points.detail: Promoting linguistic innovation, negotiating social taboos, building rapport, and signalling who belongs to the group and who doesn't.

questions.q: Explain how informal language promotes linguistic innovation and helps negotiate social taboos, giving an example of each.
answer: Informal contexts tolerate novelty, so neologisms, blends and new slang emerge and spread there first.
Example: internet-origin coinages entering everyday speech before any dictionary records them.
Taboo topics are negotiated through euphemism, dysphemism and humour, letting participants discuss the difficult.
Example: joking dysphemism about illness or death, which manages discomfort while allowing the subject to be raised.

points.title: Cohesion and coherence in informal texts
points.detail: The discourse factors that hold an informal text together, and why a text can be cohesive without being coherent or the reverse.

questions.q: Explain why an informal conversation between close friends may have low cohesion but remain highly coherent for its participants.
answer: Shared context means much is left implicit — ellipsis, deixis and unexplained references reduce surface cohesion.
Participants supply the missing links through inference from shared knowledge.
Coherence depends on whether it makes sense to its audience, not on explicit linking devices.
An outsider reading the same transcript may find it incoherent.

card.title: Cohesion — the devices
card.front: Name the cohesive devices that tie a text together.
back: Lexical choice — synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy, hypernymy, collocation
Reference — anaphoric (back), cataphoric (forward), deictics
Substitution and ellipsis — avoid repeating what’s recoverable
Conjunctions and adverbials — signal logical links
Information flow — clefting, front focus, end focus
Repetition — of word, structure or sound

points.title: Transcription conventions
points.detail: The conventions for transcribing spoken English — symbols, legend and line numbers — and referring to line numbers accurately in an analysis.

questions.q: A transcript line reads: '12 A: so (.) i mean it's not [that] bad'. Explain what each convention represents.
answer: '12' is the line number, used for accurate reference in an analysis.
'(.)' marks a micropause — a brief pause too short to time.
'[' marks the onset of overlapping speech with another speaker.
Always quote line numbers when referring to a transcript in your answer.

points.title: The role of Standard English in formal texts
points.detail: How SAE carries prestige in formal contexts, and what its use signals about the writer or speaker.

questions.q: Explain what a writer's use of Standard English in a formal text signals to the reader, and why the variety carries that force.
answer: It signals authority, credibility and membership of educated institutional discourse.
SAE carries overt prestige because it is the codified variety used by powerful institutions.
That prestige is a social fact, not a linguistic one — SAE is not inherently clearer or more logical.
Departing from it in a formal text risks the writer being judged as less competent.

points.title: Functions of language in formal texts
points.detail: The same six functions, but identifying how they operate in planned, edited and often public language.

questions.q: Identify the dominant function of language in a public health advertisement and explain how a second function supports it.
answer: Conative is dominant — the text directs the audience to change behaviour.
Referential support: statistics or medical information establish the basis for the instruction.
Poetic function may also operate through slogans, alliteration or rhythm making the message memorable.

points.title: Register, tenor and audience in formal texts
points.detail: How anticipating an audience's interpretation shapes formal choices, and how tenor sets the degree of formality.

questions.q: Explain how anticipating an unknown, public audience shapes the language of a formal written text.
answer: Context cannot be assumed, so the text must be explicit — low deixis, few unexplained references.
Interpretation cannot be checked in real time, so cohesion and structure must be strong.
The widest plausible audience is addressed, so specialised terms are defined or avoided.
Face needs of a diverse audience are managed through non-discriminatory language and hedging.

points.title: Context and language features in formal texts
points.detail: The relationship between situational and cultural context and the features that appear — including what the context makes explicit that an informal text would leave assumed.

questions.q: Explain how the situational context of a government media release shapes its language features.
answer: Tenor: distant and institutional, requiring formality and negative politeness.
Field: policy or administrative matter, drawing on jargon and specialised lexis.
Mode: written, planned and edited, producing complex syntax and strong cohesion.
The audience is unknown and public, so context must be made explicit rather than assumed — and language may be chosen to obscure as well as clarify.

card.title: How context shapes features
card.front: Link situational context to the features that appear — informal and formal.
back: Field — the subject matter drives the lexis and any jargon
Tenor — relationship and social distance set the politeness and formality
Mode — spoken or written changes planning, cohesion and non-fluency
Setting — public or private, immediate or distant audience
Informal: shared context means more can be left implicit
Formal: context must be made explicit for an unknown audience

points.title: Features of formal writing
points.detail: Greater cohesion, editing, explicitness about context, complex syntax and nominalisation — and the capacity to be deliberately ambiguous.

questions.q: Identify four features of formal written language and explain what each signals.
answer: Standard English and careful editing — signals authority and credibility.
Complex syntax with subordination — allows precise qualification of claims.
Nominalisation — raises formality and can remove the actor from the clause.
Specialised lexis or jargon — establishes expertise and assumes an informed reader.
Also acceptable: explicitness, low deixis, strong cohesive linking.

card.title: Features of formal writing
card.front: What marks a written text as formal?
back: Standard English throughout, edited and proofread
Complex syntax, subordination, nominalisation
Precise, often specialised or technical lexis; jargon
Explicit — context spelled out for an unknown audience
Strong cohesion and clear structure
Can be deliberately ambiguous or evasive when it suits

points.title: Features of formal speech
points.detail: Formal speech carrying the organisational features of written language while still drawing on prosody and paralinguistic features; rehearsal and editing.

questions.q: Explain how a formal speech differs from both spontaneous speech and formal writing.
answer: Unlike spontaneous speech, it is rehearsed and edited, so non-fluency is minimal and structure is planned.
It carries written-language organisation: full clauses, clear sections, strong cohesion.
Unlike formal writing, it retains prosody and paralinguistics — pitch, stress, pause and gesture used deliberately for effect.
It sits between the two modes rather than belonging wholly to either.

card.title: Features of formal speech
card.front: What marks a spoken text as formal?
back: Rehearsed, edited, sometimes read from a script
Written-language organisation: clear structure, full clauses
Non-fluency minimised; prosody used deliberately for effect
Standard pronunciation; fewer connected speech processes
Still draws on prosodic and paralinguistic features to persuade

points.title: Features of spoken discourse in formal texts
points.detail: How the discourse features of speech appear, or are suppressed, in a planned formal spoken text.

questions.q: Explain how turn-taking and topic management differ in a courtroom exchange compared with a casual conversation.
answer: Turn-taking rights are allocated by role — the barrister questions, the witness answers.
Topic control sits with the more powerful participant; the witness cannot introduce a new topic.
Interruption is marked and often sanctioned rather than supportive.
This reflects the institutional tenor and the unequal power relationship.

card.title: Spoken discourse in informal and formal texts
card.front: Which discourse features appear, and which get suppressed, in each?
back: Informal — openings/closings loose, overlap common, non-fluency frequent
Informal — adjacency pairs casual, backchannels constant
Formal — turns allocated by role, overlap rare, non-fluency edited out
Formal — planned openings and closings, explicit topic management
Formal speech carries written-language organisation with spoken delivery

points.title: Subsystem patterning and rhetoric
points.detail: Patterning across the subsystems used rhetorically — syntactic patterning such as antithesis, listing and parallelism, and phonological patterning.

questions.q: A speech includes: 'We have the resources. We have the expertise. We have the will.' Analyse the patterning used and its persuasive effect.
answer: Syntactic parallelism: three clauses of identical structure.
Repetition (anaphora) of 'We have the' at the start of each.
Tricolon: the three-part structure creates rhythm and a sense of completeness.
Effect: builds cumulative force, and the inclusive 'we' aligns speaker with audience, making the conclusion feel inevitable.

card.title: Subsystem patterning and rhetoric
card.front: How is patterning used rhetorically in formal texts?
back: Phonological — alliteration, rhythm to make a line stick
Syntactic — antithesis, listing, parallelism for force and balance
Semantic — metaphor, hyperbole, irony to frame the issue
Rhetoric works across subsystems at once in a single line
State the persuasive purpose, not just the device name

points.title: Jargon, euphemism, doublespeak and non-discriminatory language
points.detail: Jargon establishing expertise or excluding outsiders, euphemism negotiating taboo, doublespeak obscuring, and non-discriminatory language as a deliberate choice.

questions.q: Distinguish euphemism from doublespeak, and explain the different purposes each serves in public language.
answer: Euphemism substitutes a milder term for one considered harsh or taboo, usually to protect face.
Doublespeak deliberately obscures or reverses meaning to conceal an unwelcome reality.
Euphemism: 'passed away' for died — softening for the hearer's benefit.
Doublespeak: 'rightsizing' for mass redundancy — protecting the speaker, not the hearer.

points.title: Discourse strategies and cooperation in formal contexts
points.detail: How cooperation is managed when roles and turn-taking rights are unequal.

questions.q: Explain how politeness strategies are used to manage the power imbalance in a formal workplace email from an employee to a senior manager.
answer: Negative politeness dominates: hedging, modality and apology minimise imposition.
Indirect requests ('I was wondering whether') give the manager an easy refusal.
Formal address terms and full standard forms acknowledge the status difference.
The greater the social distance and power gap, the more mitigation is required.

card.title: Discourse strategies in formal contexts
card.front: How is cooperation managed when roles and rights are unequal?
back: Turn-taking rights allocated by role — chair, interviewer, judge
Topic control sits with the more powerful participant
Interruption is marked and often face-threatening
Repair is more explicit and more costly to face
Politeness strategies mitigate the imbalance

points.title: Formality for distance, authority and expertise
points.detail: Politeness strategies in formal texts, reinforcing social distance and hierarchy, and establishing expertise and authority.

questions.q: Explain how formal language reinforces social distance and establishes expertise, naming one feature that achieves each.
answer: Social distance: negative politeness and formal address terms mark the participants as non-intimate.
Feature: modality and hedging ('it may be appropriate to consider') avoid direct imposition.
Expertise: jargon and specialised lexis signal membership of a professional field.
Jargon simultaneously establishes authority for insiders and excludes those outside the field.

points.title: Formality for harmony, taboo and obfuscation
points.detail: Promoting social harmony, negotiating social taboos and building rapport, and the clarify–manipulate–obfuscate range, particularly in public language.

questions.q: A company statement reads: 'Regrettably, a small number of accounts may have been subject to unauthorised access.' Analyse how the language manages the situation.
answer: Agentless passive 'may have been subject to' removes the company as actor, obscuring responsibility.
Modality 'may' and the minimiser 'a small number' reduce the apparent scale.
'Unauthorised access' is a euphemism for a data breach.
The text sits toward the obfuscation end of the clarify–manipulate–obfuscate range while appearing to disclose.

points.title: Cohesion and coherence in formal texts
points.detail: The discourse factors creating cohesion and coherence, and why formal texts usually score higher on both.

questions.q: Explain why formal written texts typically show higher cohesion than informal spoken texts.
answer: Formal texts are planned and edited, so cohesive devices can be deliberately inserted.
The audience is unknown and absent, so links must be made explicit rather than inferred.
Conjunctive adverbials, clear reference chains and consistent lexical fields do the work that shared context does in conversation.
Informal speech relies on inference and deixis instead.

card.title: Coherence — the factors
card.front: What makes a text coherent, and how does it differ from cohesion?
back: Cohesion is the surface glue; coherence is whether it makes sense
Inference — the reader supplies what isn’t stated
Logical ordering — the sequence matches the content
Formatting — headings, paragraphs, layout guiding the reader
Consistency and conventions — the text behaves as its type should
A text can be cohesive and incoherent, or coherent with little cohesion

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Standard Australian English and its role
points.detail: The features that distinguish SAE, and how public institutions afford it prestige in Australian society.

questions.q: Explain what gives Standard Australian English its status, and why describing other varieties as 'incorrect' is a prescriptivist position.
answer: SAE is codified in dictionaries, grammars and style guides and used by institutions — education, government, media.
Its status is social and historical, not a property of the variety itself.
Other varieties are systematic and rule-governed, with their own consistent patterns.
Calling them incorrect applies SAE's norms as a universal standard, which is prescriptivism.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Identities conveyed in Australian texts
points.detail: The ways a variety of identities are conveyed and reflected in written and spoken Australian texts.

questions.q: Explain how a text can convey an Australian identity, naming two linguistic features and their effect.
answer: Lexis: distinctly Australian terms and hypocoristics (arvo, servo, ute) signal shared cultural knowledge.
Phonology: Australian vowels and non-rhoticity mark the speaker as local.
Discourse: understatement, self-deprecation and the levelling of status markers.
Together these construct an identity recognisable to insiders and often stereotyped by outsiders.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Broad, General and Cultivated accents
points.detail: The evolution of the three Australian accent groups, their phonological features, and the attitudes attached to each.

questions.q: Describe the three Australian accent groups and explain how attitudes to them have shifted.
answer: Broad — strongest Australian features, historically associated with rural and working-class speakers.
General — the most widely used variety, occupying the middle of the continuum.
Cultivated — closest to Received Pronunciation, historically associated with prestige and education.
Cultivated has declined and now sometimes attracts negative judgement as affected, while Broad carries covert prestige as authentically Australian.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Cultural variation in Australian English
points.detail: How English varies according to culture — Standard Australian English, Aboriginal Australian Englishes and migrant ethnolects, and the features that mark each.

questions.q: Name three varieties of English used in Australia and describe one distinguishing feature of each.
answer: Standard Australian English — codified, used in education, government and media.
Aboriginal Australian Englishes — a continuum drawing on First Nations languages, contact language and non-standard English features.
Migrant ethnolects — combine Australian English with features of a community's first language.
All three are systematic varieties; the differences are patterned, not random.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Attitudes to varieties of English
points.detail: Attitudes within Australian society to different varieties, including prescriptivist and descriptivist positions, and what those attitudes reveal about the holder.

questions.q: A talkback caller complains that young people 'are ruining the language'. Identify the position taken and write a descriptivist response.
answer: Prescriptivist — treating one variety as correct and change as decay.
Descriptivist response: language change is constant, systematic and observable in every period.
Features now considered standard were themselves once condemned as errors.
The task of linguistics is to describe how language is used, not to rule on how it should be.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Global contact and modern technologies
points.detail: How English in Australia is being shaped by global contact, technology and other social change.

questions.q: Explain two ways global contact and modern technologies are changing Australian English, with an example of each.
answer: Borrowing and Americanisation: American lexis and spellings spread through media and software defaults.
Technology-driven innovation: new coinages and abbreviations originate online and move into speech.
Convergence: exposure to global varieties reduces some distinctly Australian features.
Speed of spread has increased — an innovation can be national within weeks rather than years.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Language and national identity
points.detail: The role of language in conveying a perceived national identity, and why that identity is contested rather than settled.

questions.q: Explain how language conveys a perceived national identity, and why that identity is contested.
answer: Shared lexis, accent and discourse conventions construct a recognisable national variety.
Certain features become emblematic — hypocoristics, understatement, the 'fair go' register of egalitarianism.
Contested because the identity constructed often reflects only some Australians.
It can exclude First Nations peoples and migrant communities whose varieties are equally Australian.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 1 — Language variation in Australian society
points.title: Stereotypes and their validity
points.detail: Language features associated with emerging and established stereotypes, adopted consciously or subconsciously, and challenging the validity of those associations.

questions.q: A commentator claims that speakers of a Broad Australian accent 'sound uneducated'. Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of language attitudes.
answer: This is a stereotype: a feature associated with a group and generalised to individuals.
Accent is not correlated with intelligence or education — it is a systematic phonological variety.
The judgement reflects overt prestige attached to more standard varieties, not linguistic fact.
Variation within any accent group exceeds the variation between groups, so the generalisation fails.

card.title: Stereotypes and their validity
card.front: Language and stereotypes — what is the argument, and how do you challenge it?
back: Features get associated with groups — Broad accent, ethnolects, teen slang
Adopted consciously to perform an identity, or subconsciously
Stereotypes are generalisations, not reliable claims about individuals
They carry covert prestige for insiders and stigma from outsiders
Challenge: variation WITHIN a group exceeds variation BETWEEN groups

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities
points.title: Sociolects and idiolects
points.detail: Social and personal variation according to age, gender, sexuality, occupation, interests, aspirations and education.

questions.q: Define sociolect and idiolect, and explain why an individual belongs to several sociolects at once.
answer: Sociolect: variation associated with a social group — age, occupation, interest, education, gender.
Idiolect: the unique combination of features used by one individual at a point in their life.
A person belongs simultaneously to groups defined by age, workplace, interests and region.
Their idiolect draws on all of these, and shifts as those group memberships change.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities
points.title: Representations of identity in texts
points.detail: How individual and group identities are represented across a range of written and spoken texts.

questions.q: Explain how a text can represent a group identity, using the concepts of lexis and discourse.
answer: Shared lexis — jargon, slang or in-group terms that only members fully interpret.
Discourse features — shared conventions for openings, humour, turn-taking and topic.
These construct the boundary of the group, marking who is inside and who is not.
Representation may be produced by the group itself, or imposed on it by outsiders through stereotype.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities
points.title: Social expectations and community attitudes
points.detail: The ways the language of individuals and of groups is shaped by what the surrounding community expects and accepts.

questions.q: Explain how community expectations shape an individual's language choices in a workplace, and what happens when those expectations are breached.
answer: Communities establish norms for register, taboo and politeness appropriate to each setting.
Individuals shift within their repertoire to meet the expectation — more formal register, less slang, more mitigation.
Breaching the norm carries social cost: loss of credibility, exclusion, or formal sanction.
Conforming earns acceptance and access to the group's resources.

card.title: Social expectations and community attitudes
card.front: How do social expectations shape the language of individuals and groups?
back: Communities set norms for register, taboo and politeness in each setting
Breaching a norm carries social cost; conforming earns acceptance
Expectations differ across workplace, family, online and school
Attitudes to non-standard varieties pressure speakers toward SAE
Individuals shift within their repertoire to meet the expectation

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities
points.title: Linguistic repertoire, power and prestige
points.detail: How people draw on their repertoire to gain power and prestige, including exploiting overt and covert norms.

questions.q: Explain how a speaker might use their linguistic repertoire to gain prestige in two different contexts, referring to both overt and covert prestige.
answer: Repertoire is the range of varieties and registers a speaker can draw on.
In a job interview, shifting toward SAE and formal register claims overt prestige and institutional authority.
Among a peer group, using slang or a local variety claims covert prestige and signals solidarity.
A wider repertoire means more situations can be navigated successfully.

card.title: Linguistic repertoire, power and prestige
card.front: How do speakers use their repertoire to gain power and prestige?
back: Repertoire — the full range of varieties and registers a speaker controls
Shifting toward SAE claims authority and overt prestige
Shifting toward local forms claims solidarity and covert prestige
Jargon claims expertise and excludes outsiders
A wider repertoire means more social situations navigable

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities
points.title: Overt and covert prestige
points.detail: Overt prestige attached to standard varieties and covert prestige attached to local forms, and how both can be deliberately used.

questions.q: Define overt and covert prestige and explain how one speaker might pursue both in a single day.
answer: Overt prestige attaches to the standard variety, recognised publicly and institutionally.
Covert prestige attaches to non-standard forms, valued within a group for signalling authenticity.
In a job interview the speaker shifts toward SAE, claiming overt prestige.
With friends afterwards they use slang and a broader accent, claiming covert prestige. Both are strategic uses of one repertoire.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities
points.title: Code switching and belonging
points.detail: Code switching as a means of demonstrating group membership and belonging, rather than as a deficiency.

questions.q: Explain why code switching is evidence of linguistic skill rather than deficiency.
answer: Code switching requires competence in more than one variety and the judgement to know when each fits.
Switches are typically rule-governed and occur at grammatically permissible points.
It is used purposefully — to signal group membership, express an idea unavailable in the other code, or include a listener.
Treating it as confusion applies a monolingual standard to multilingual competence.

points.area: Unit 4 AoS 2 — Individual and group identities
points.title: Social attitudes, language choices and discrimination
points.detail: The relationship between social attitudes and language choices, and how personal associations and prejudices can lead to social disadvantage and discrimination.

questions.q: Explain how attitudes toward a language variety can result in social disadvantage, with reference to a specific context.
answer: Attitudes toward a variety transfer onto its speakers, who are judged on competence or character.
In employment, a candidate speaking a stigmatised ethnolect may be rated less favourably despite equal qualifications.
Consequences extend to education, housing and treatment in the justice system.
Linguistic prejudice often operates as an acceptable proxy for racial or class prejudice.

card.title: Social attitudes and discrimination
card.front: How do language attitudes lead to disadvantage?
back: Attitudes to a variety transfer onto its speakers
Non-standard varieties judged as less intelligent or less competent
Consequences in employment, education, housing, the justice system
Linguistic prejudice is often the socially acceptable cover for other bias
Speakers may abandon a variety to avoid the cost

points.title: Connected speech processes
points.detail: Assimilation, vowel reduction, elision and insertion — identifying them in a transcript and explaining what they signal about formality and planning.

questions.q: In a transcript, a speaker produces 'goin' to the shops' and 'han(d)bag'. Identify the connected speech process in each case and explain what their presence suggests about the exchange.
answer: 'goin'' — elision: the final consonant of the -ing cluster is dropped.
'han(d)bag' — elision of /d/ in the consonant cluster.
Both suggest rapid, spontaneous, informal speech.
They indicate low planning and reduced social distance, not careless or incorrect speech.

card.title: Connected speech processes
card.front: What are the four connected speech processes, and what do they signal?
back: Assimilation — a sound shifts to match a neighbour: “ten bikes” → /tem baɪks/
Vowel reduction — full vowel becomes schwa /ə/ in unstressed syllables
Elision — a sound is dropped: “friendship” → /frenʃɪp/
Insertion — an extra sound appears: “warmth” → /wɔːmpθ/
All four signal speed, spontaneity and informality — not carelessness

points.title: The IPA and transcription of Australian English
points.detail: Reading and writing IPA transcriptions of Australian English as described by Harrington, Cox & Evans.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by saying Australian English is non-rhotic, and give one example using IPA.
answer: The /r/ phoneme is not pronounced when it follows a vowel and is not followed by another vowel.
'car' is /kaː/ rather than /kaːr/.
Also acceptable: 'farm' /faːm/, 'water' /woːtə/.

card.title: IPA and transcribing Australian English
card.front: What do you need to get right when transcribing Australian English?
back: Phonemic transcription sits inside slashes / /
Australian English is non-rhotic — no /r/ after a vowel: “car” = /kaː/
Stress marked with ˈ immediately before the stressed syllable
Watch the vowels — /æ/ vs /e/, and the diphthongs /æɪ/ /ɑe/ /æɔ/
Cox and Evans is the description the study design names

points.title: Prosodic features
points.detail: Pitch, stress, volume, tempo and intonation, and the meaning each carries in a spoken text.

questions.q: A speaker delivers a line with rising intonation at the end of a declarative and stress placed on the final word. Explain what each prosodic feature contributes to the meaning.
answer: Rising intonation on a declarative (HRT) can seek agreement, signal uncertainty, or invite the listener to respond.
Stress on the final word foregrounds it as the most important information in the utterance.
Together they can soften an assertion and reduce the face threat of disagreeing.
Name the feature AND state its function — not the label alone.

card.title: Prosodic vs paralinguistic features
card.front: What belongs to prosody, what belongs to paralinguistics, and what does each do?
back: Prosody is IN the voice: pitch, stress, volume, tempo, intonation
Rising intonation (HRT) — question, uncertainty, or seeking agreement
Stress shifts focus; tempo and volume carry urgency and emotion
Paralinguistics is AROUND the voice: laughter, crying, creaky voice, breathiness
Non-verbal: gesture, facial expression, eye contact, posture
Both carry meaning a bare transcript cannot show

points.title: Phonological patterning
points.detail: Alliteration, assonance, consonance, onomatopoeia, rhythm and rhyme — and what the patterning achieves rather than just naming it.

questions.q: A public health slogan reads 'Slow down, stay safe, save lives'. Identify one phonological and one syntactic patterning feature and explain the effect of each.
answer: Phonological — alliteration of /s/ across 'slow', 'stay', 'safe', 'save': memorability and cohesion.
Syntactic — parallelism: three imperative verb phrases of matching structure.
The rhythm of the tricolon gives the slogan force and makes it easy to recall.
Marks require the effect, not just the identification.

card.title: Phonological patterning
card.front: Name the phonological patterning devices — and the effect of each.
back: Alliteration — repeated initial consonant; memorability, cohesion
Assonance — repeated vowel sounds
Consonance — repeated consonants, not only initial
Onomatopoeia — the sound imitates the sense
Rhythm and rhyme — pace, playfulness, memorability
Never stop at the label — always state what the patterning achieves

points.title: Word formation processes
points.detail: Affixation, abbreviation, shortening, compounding, blending, backformation, conversion of word class, initialism, acronym and contraction.

questions.q: Identify the word formation process used to create each of the following: 'brunch', 'ANZAC', 'to medal' (as in to win a medal), 'servo'.
answer: 'brunch' — blending of breakfast and lunch.
'ANZAC' — acronym: pronounced as a word, not letter by letter.
'to medal' — conversion of word class, noun to verb.
'servo' — shortening with hypocoristic -o suffix.

card.title: Word formation processes
card.front: How are new words formed? Name each process with an example.
back: Affixation (un-, -ness) · compounding (laptop) · blending (brunch)
Shortening (uni) · contraction (don’t) · abbreviation
Initialism = said letter by letter (ATM); acronym = said as a word (ANZAC)
Backformation (edit ← editor) · conversion of word class (to google)
Hypocoristics — the -ie/-o suffix (mozzie, arvo, servo)
Hypocoristics are distinctively Australian: informality and solidarity

points.title: Hypocoristic use of suffixes
points.detail: The Australian pattern of mozzie, sickie, tradie — same denotation as the original, different connotation and formality.

questions.q: Explain what hypocoristics are, give two Australian examples, and describe their social function.
answer: Hypocoristics shorten a word and add a suffix, usually -ie/-y or -o.
Examples: mozzie, arvo, tradie, barbie, servo.
They mark informality and signal solidarity and shared Australian identity.
They carry the same denotation as the full form but different connotation.

card.title: Word formation processes
card.front: How are new words formed? Name each process with an example.
back: Affixation (un-, -ness) · compounding (laptop) · blending (brunch)
Shortening (uni) · contraction (don’t) · abbreviation
Initialism = said letter by letter (ATM); acronym = said as a word (ANZAC)
Backformation (edit ← editor) · conversion of word class (to google)
Hypocoristics — the -ie/-o suffix (mozzie, arvo, servo)
Hypocoristics are distinctively Australian: informality and solidarity

points.title: Word classes
points.detail: Nouns including pronouns; verbs including auxiliary and modal verbs; adjectives; adverbs; prepositions; conjunctions (coordinators and subordinators); determiners; interjections.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The council may consider the proposal next month', identify the modal verb, the determiner and the adverbial, and explain what the modal contributes.
answer: Modal verb: 'may'. Determiner: 'The'. Adverbial: 'next month'.
The modal expresses possibility rather than certainty.
It hedges the commitment, leaving the council free not to act — a negative politeness or evasion strategy.

card.title: Word classes
card.front: Name the word classes and what each does.
back: Nouns — including pronouns; name entities
Verbs — including auxiliary and modal verbs; modals carry obligation and certainty
Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, whole clauses
Prepositions show relationship in space, time or logic
Conjunctions — coordinators (and, but) and subordinators (because, although)
Determiners specify reference; interjections carry emotion

points.title: Lexical word formation and loss
points.detail: Neologism, borrowings, commonisation and nominalisation.

questions.q: Identify the process of lexical change in each: 'esky' used for any portable cooler; 'the government's implementation of the policy'; 'doomscrolling'.
answer: 'esky' — commonisation: a proper noun (brand name) becoming a common noun.
'implementation' — nominalisation: the verb 'implement' converted to a noun.
'doomscrolling' — neologism, formed by compounding.
Nominalisation raises formality and removes the actor from the clause.

card.title: Lexical change
card.front: Four ways the lexicon changes, beyond word formation.
back: Neologism — a brand new word, or a new sense for an old one
Borrowing — taken from another language (yakka, tsunami)
Commonisation — a proper noun becomes a common noun (esky, google)
Nominalisation — verb or adjective becomes a noun (decide → decision)
Nominalisation raises formality and conveniently deletes the actor
Also obsolescence — words falling out of use

points.title: Phrases
points.detail: Noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, adverb phrase and prepositional phrase — identifying them and naming their head.

questions.q: Identify the head of the noun phrase 'the recently approved planning application' and explain what the length of this phrase suggests about the text's register.
answer: Head: 'application'.
'the', 'recently approved' and 'planning' are all premodifiers.
Heavily premodified noun phrases are characteristic of formal, written, often bureaucratic register.

card.title: Phrases
card.front: The five phrase types — how do you identify one?
back: A phrase is named after its head word
Noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, adverb phrase, prepositional phrase
A phrase can be a single word or many
Long premodified noun phrases are a marker of formal writing
Identify the head first, then the modifiers around it

points.title: Clauses
points.detail: Functions within the clause — subject, object, predicate, complement, adverbial — and combining clauses through coordination and subordination.

questions.q: Classify the sentence 'Although the deadline had passed, the committee accepted the submission because the delay was explained' by structure, and identify the subordinating conjunctions.
answer: Complex sentence — one main clause with two subordinate clauses.
Main clause: 'the committee accepted the submission'.
Subordinating conjunctions: 'Although' and 'because'.
A high density of subordination is a marker of formal written register.

card.title: Clauses
card.front: Clause functions and how clauses combine.
back: Subject — who or what the clause is about
Predicate — everything said about the subject
Object, complement and adverbial — the other clause elements
Coordination joins clauses of equal status
Subordination makes one clause dependent on another
Subordination density rises with formality

points.title: Sentence structures and types
points.detail: Fragments; simple, compound, complex and compound-complex structures. Declarative, imperative, interrogative and exclamative types, and their communicative function.

questions.q: Classify each by structure and by type: 'Stop.' / 'Although it rained, the match continued, and the crowd stayed.' / 'What time does it start?'
answer: 'Stop.' — simple structure, imperative type.
'Although it rained, the match continued, and the crowd stayed.' — compound-complex; declarative.
'What time does it start?' — simple structure, interrogative type.
Structure counts clauses; type identifies communicative function. Both are needed.

points.title: Word order
points.detail: Subject–verb–object, modifiers within a noun phrase, and the placement of adverbials — including what a departure from expected order achieves.

questions.q: A speaker says: 'Never in my life have I seen anything like it.' Identify the departure from standard word order and explain its effect.
answer: Fronting of the adverbial 'Never in my life', with subject–auxiliary inversion following.
Standard order would be 'I have never seen anything like it'.
The marked order foregrounds the adverbial, giving emphasis and heightening the emotional force.
It also raises the register — inversion of this kind is rare in casual speech.

card.title: Word order
card.front: Standard word order in English, and what a departure achieves.
back: Subject–verb–object is the unmarked English order
Modifiers sit in a conventional order inside the noun phrase
Adverbials are the most mobile element
Marked order foregrounds information — fronting, clefting, inversion
Departures draw attention: state what is being emphasised

points.title: Active and passive voice
points.detail: Including agentless passives, and why a writer might choose to remove the agent.

questions.q: A media release states: 'Errors were made in the processing of applications.' Identify the voice used, explain what the construction achieves, and rewrite it in the active voice.
answer: Agentless passive — 'were made' with no 'by' phrase identifying who made the errors.
It removes the actor, so responsibility is obscured while the error is acknowledged.
It also raises formality and depersonalises the statement.
Active: 'We made errors in processing applications' — or name the responsible party.

card.title: Active and passive voice
card.front: How does the passive work, and why choose it?
back: Active — the agent is the subject and is doing the verb
Passive — the patient becomes the subject; agent moves to a “by” phrase
Agentless passive deletes the actor entirely (“mistakes were made”)
Uses: raise formality, shift focus, obscure responsibility
A favourite of public language and doublespeak

points.title: Syntactic patterning
points.detail: Antithesis, listing and parallelism, and the rhetorical effect each produces.

questions.q: A politician says: 'We were not elected to manage decline; we were elected to build.' Identify the syntactic patterning and explain its rhetorical effect.
answer: Antithesis — two contrasting ideas placed in a parallel grammatical structure.
Parallelism reinforces it: 'we were elected to...' repeated across both clauses.
The balance makes the contrast memorable and frames the second option as obviously preferable.
It also creates an in-group 'we' aligning speaker and audience.

card.title: Syntactic patterning
card.front: The three syntactic patterning devices: define each and give its effect.
back: Antithesis — contrasting ideas in parallel structure (“not X, but Y”)
Listing — accumulation; builds weight or a sense of completeness
Parallelism — repeated grammatical structure across clauses
Effects: rhetorical force, balance, emphasis, memorability
Turns up constantly in speeches and public language

points.title: Paralinguistic features
points.detail: Vocal effects including whispers and laughter; non-verbal communication including gesture, facial expression and eye contact; creakiness and breathiness.

questions.q: A transcript notes (laughs) and (creaky voice) alongside the spoken text. Explain what these annotations are recording and why they matter to an analysis.
answer: Both are paralinguistic features — vocal effects accompanying speech rather than prosodic properties of it.
They carry meaning the words alone do not: laughter can soften a face-threatening act or signal solidarity.
Creaky voice may mark the end of a turn or a particular social identity.

card.title: Prosodic vs paralinguistic features
card.front: What belongs to prosody, what belongs to paralinguistics, and what does each do?
back: Prosody is IN the voice: pitch, stress, volume, tempo, intonation
Rising intonation (HRT) — question, uncertainty, or seeking agreement
Stress shifts focus; tempo and volume carry urgency and emotion
Paralinguistics is AROUND the voice: laughter, crying, creaky voice, breathiness
Non-verbal: gesture, facial expression, eye contact, posture
Both carry meaning a bare transcript cannot show

points.title: Transcription conventions
points.detail: The symbols, legend and line numbering used for transcribing spoken language, and reading them accurately under exam pressure.

questions.q: Explain what (2.0), = and ↗ conventionally represent in a transcript, and why the legend matters.
answer: (2.0) — a timed pause of two seconds.
= — latching, where one turn follows immediately with no gap.
↗ — rising intonation on the following segment.
Conventions vary between transcripts, so the legend supplied with the text governs interpretation.

points.title: Cohesion
points.detail: Lexical choice (synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy, hypernymy), collocation, information flow (clefting, front focus, end focus), anaphoric and cataphoric reference, deictics, repetition, substitution, ellipsis, conjunctions and adverbials.

questions.q: Identify four cohesive devices in the following and name each: 'The council released the report. It recommended three changes. However, these were rejected. The decision disappointed residents.'
answer: 'It' — anaphoric reference back to 'the report'.
'However' — a conjunctive adverbial signalling contrast.
'these' — anaphoric reference to 'three changes'.
'The decision' — lexical cohesion, summarising the previous clause with a related noun.
Also acceptable: collocation across 'council', 'report', 'recommended'.

card.title: Cohesion — the devices
card.front: Name the cohesive devices that tie a text together.
back: Lexical choice — synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy, hypernymy, collocation
Reference — anaphoric (back), cataphoric (forward), deictics
Substitution and ellipsis — avoid repeating what’s recoverable
Conjunctions and adverbials — signal logical links
Information flow — clefting, front focus, end focus
Repetition — of word, structure or sound

points.title: Coherence
points.detail: Cohesion, inference, logical ordering, formatting, and consistency and conventions — and the difference between coherence and cohesion.

questions.q: Explain the difference between cohesion and coherence, and describe how a text could be cohesive but incoherent.
answer: Cohesion is the surface linking of a text through reference, conjunctions, ellipsis and lexical choice.
Coherence is whether the text makes sense as a whole to its reader.
A text can chain pronouns and conjunctions correctly while the ideas do not follow logically.
Coherence also depends on inference, logical ordering, formatting and conventions.

card.title: Coherence — the factors
card.front: What makes a text coherent, and how does it differ from cohesion?
back: Cohesion is the surface glue; coherence is whether it makes sense
Inference — the reader supplies what isn’t stated
Logical ordering — the sequence matches the content
Formatting — headings, paragraphs, layout guiding the reader
Consistency and conventions — the text behaves as its type should
A text can be cohesive and incoherent, or coherent with little cohesion

points.title: Features of spoken discourse
points.detail: Openings and closings, adjacency pairs, minimal responses and backchannels, overlapping speech, discourse markers and particles, and non-fluency features including pauses, filled pauses, false starts, repetition and repairs.

questions.q: A transcript shows: A: 'so anyway (0.5) um the thing is—' B: 'mm' A: 'the thing is we can't afford it'. Identify three features of spoken discourse present.
answer: Discourse markers: 'so', 'anyway'.
Non-fluency: a filled pause 'um', a pause (0.5), a false start and self-repair on 'the thing is—'.
Minimal response / backchannel: B's 'mm', signalling active listening without taking the floor.
Repetition of 'the thing is' is the repair completing the abandoned utterance.

card.title: Features of spoken discourse
card.front: The structural features of spontaneous speech.
back: Openings and closings — conventional ways in and out
Adjacency pairs — greeting/greeting, question/answer, offer/accept
Minimal responses and backchannels signal listening
Overlapping speech — supportive or competitive
Discourse markers and particles signal structure and stance
Non-fluency: pauses, filled pauses, false starts, repetition, repairs

points.title: Strategies in spoken discourse
points.detail: Topic management, turn-taking, management of repair sequences, and code switching as a marker of group membership.

questions.q: Distinguish between features of spoken discourse and strategies in spoken discourse, giving one example of each.
answer: Features are what appears in the text: discourse markers, non-fluency, adjacency pairs, backchannels.
Strategies are what speakers DO with those features to manage the interaction.
Feature example: overlapping speech. Strategy example: turn-taking — claiming or yielding the floor.
Also strategies: topic management, repair, code switching.

card.title: Strategies in spoken discourse
card.front: The strategies speakers use to manage an interaction.
back: Topic management — introducing, developing, shifting, closing
Turn-taking — holding, yielding and claiming the floor
Repair — fixing a breakdown in understanding, self or other
Code switching — marks group membership and shared identity
Features are what appears; strategies are what speakers DO with them

points.title: Politeness strategies
points.detail: Positive and negative face, positive and negative face-threatening acts, and positive and negative politeness.

questions.q: A colleague writes: 'Sorry to bother you — I don't suppose you'd have a moment to look at this, if you get a chance?' Identify the politeness strategies and explain which face need they address.
answer: Negative politeness — the writer avoids imposing.
Apology ('sorry to bother you'), hedging ('I don't suppose', 'if you get a chance') and modality ('would').
These address the reader's negative face: the want to be unimpeded and free from imposition.
The request is a face-threatening act, and the mitigation reduces the threat.

card.title: Politeness, face and face-threatening acts
card.front: Brown and Levinson’s politeness theory — the whole model.
back: Face = public self-image that everyone wants respected
Positive face — the want to be liked, approved of, included
Negative face — the want to be unimpeded and not imposed upon
A face-threatening act (FTA) damages one or the other
Positive politeness — compliments, in-group language, agreement
Negative politeness — hedging, apology, indirectness, modals
More social distance or power difference → more mitigation

points.title: Semantic domain, inference and the sign
points.detail: The relation of meaning and sign, semantic domains as lexical sets sharing a property, and inference as meaning the audience supplies.

questions.q: A restaurant review contains 'palate', 'reduction', 'plating' and 'seasoning'. Identify what these words form and explain what it reveals about the text.
answer: They form a semantic domain (or lexical field) of food and cooking.
The domain establishes the field of the text and builds lexical cohesion.
It also signals the writer's expertise and assumes a reader who shares the register.

card.title: Sense relations and semantic domain
card.front: Define the sense relations and explain how they build cohesion.
back: Synonymy (same meaning) and antonymy (opposite)
Hyponymy — a specific member; hypernymy — the class above it
Semantic domain — a set of words sharing a field (all legal, all medical)
Denotation = dictionary meaning; connotation = the associations it carries
Idiom — meaning not derivable from the individual words
Inference — meaning the audience supplies from context

points.title: Semantic patterning
points.detail: Figurative language, irony, metaphor, oxymoron, simile, hyperbole, personification, animation, puns and lexical ambiguity.

questions.q: A news headline reads: 'Budget leaves households drowning'. Identify the semantic patterning device and explain its effect on the reader's interpretation.
answer: Metaphor — households are described as drowning, mapping financial pressure onto physical danger.
It frames the situation as urgent and life-threatening rather than merely difficult.
The connotation positions the reader to view the budget negatively.
Also acceptable: hyperbole, given the exaggeration involved.

card.title: Semantic patterning
card.front: List the semantic patterning devices and what they achieve.
back: Figurative: metaphor, simile, personification, animation, hyperbole
Irony — a gap between what is said and what is meant
Oxymoron — contradictory terms joined together
Puns and lexical ambiguity — a double meaning exploited deliberately
Effects: engagement, humour, persuasion, softening a hard message

points.title: Sense relations
points.detail: Synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy and hypernymy, idiom, and denotation versus connotation.

questions.q: Define hyponymy and antonymy, give an example of each, and explain how sense relations contribute to cohesion in a text.
answer: Hyponymy: a word whose meaning is included in a broader term — 'sedan' is a hyponym of 'vehicle'.
Antonymy: words of opposite meaning — 'increase' and 'decrease'.
Using related words across a text links sentences without repeating the same term.
This creates lexical cohesion and helps the reader follow the topic.

card.title: Sense relations and semantic domain
card.front: Define the sense relations and explain how they build cohesion.
back: Synonymy (same meaning) and antonymy (opposite)
Hyponymy — a specific member; hypernymy — the class above it
Semantic domain — a set of words sharing a field (all legal, all medical)
Denotation = dictionary meaning; connotation = the associations it carries
Idiom — meaning not derivable from the individual words
Inference — meaning the audience supplies from context

points.title: Euphemism and dysphemism
points.detail: Both as tools for negotiating taboo, and recognising that dysphemism can build solidarity as readily as it offends.

questions.q: Distinguish euphemism from dysphemism and explain how each can be used to negotiate taboo.
answer: Euphemism substitutes a milder expression for one felt to be harsh or taboo.
Dysphemism substitutes a harsher or more offensive expression than necessary.
Euphemism protects face and allows a taboo subject to be raised politely.
Dysphemism can build solidarity among intimates, or deliberately shock and offend — its effect depends on tenor.

points.title: Situational and cultural context
points.detail: Situational context as field, tenor, language mode, setting and text type. Cultural context as the values, attitudes and beliefs participants bring.

questions.q: Define field, tenor and mode, and explain how each would differ between a text message to a friend and a letter from a bank.
answer: Field — the subject matter. Personal arrangements versus financial account information.
Tenor — the relationship between participants. Close and equal versus distant and institutionally unequal.
Mode — spoken or written and the degree of planning. Spontaneous written versus planned, edited written.
These situational factors drive the lexical, syntactic and discourse choices in each text.

card.title: Situational and cultural context
card.front: Break down the two kinds of context.
back: Situational: field, tenor, mode, setting and text type
Field — subject matter; tenor — relationship between participants
Mode — spoken or written; setting — where and when
Cultural context — the shared values, attitudes and beliefs assumed
Cultural context explains why a text works for one audience and not another

points.title: Register and tenor
points.detail: Register as variation defined by use, tenor as the relationship between participants including social distance and level of formality.

questions.q: Define register and tenor and explain the relationship between them.
answer: Register is variation in language according to use — the situation it occurs in.
Tenor is the relationship between participants, covering social distance and relative power.
Tenor is one of the situational factors that determines register.
A shift in tenor, such as a manager joining a conversation, produces a shift in register.

points.title: Functions of language
points.detail: Jakobson's six: referential, emotive, conative, phatic, metalinguistic and poetic, with an example of each.

questions.q: Name Jakobson's six functions of language and give a brief example of the phatic and the metalinguistic.
answer: Referential, emotive, conative, phatic, metalinguistic, poetic.
Phatic: 'How's it going?' — maintaining the social channel rather than seeking information.
Metalinguistic: 'What do you mean by that?' — language used to talk about language itself.
Most texts operate several functions at once; identify the dominant one.

points.title: Standard English, SAE, codification and standardisation
points.detail: What makes a variety standard, how codification works through dictionaries, style guides and grammars, and the prestige that follows.

questions.q: Explain what codification is and how it contributes to a variety becoming standard.
answer: Codification is the recording of a variety's forms in dictionaries, grammars and style guides.
It fixes spellings, meanings and conventions, giving an authority to appeal to.
Institutions then adopt the codified variety in education, government, law and media.
That institutional use, not any inherent quality, is what confers prestige on the variety.

points.title: Prescriptivism and descriptivism
points.detail: The two stances on language behaviour, and identifying which one a commentator is taking from their wording.

questions.q: Define prescriptivism and descriptivism, and identify which is at work in the statement 'Literally shouldn't be used for emphasis'.
answer: Prescriptivism: judging usage against rules of correctness and advocating how language should be used.
Descriptivism: observing and recording how language is actually used, without judgement.
The statement is prescriptivist — it rules on correct usage.
A descriptivist would note the intensifying use is widespread, patterned, and parallels earlier shifts such as 'really'.

points.title: Politeness theory
points.detail: Brown and Levinson's face needs — positive and negative — face-threatening acts, and the strategies used to mitigate them.

questions.q: Define positive face and negative face, and identify which is threatened when a manager publicly corrects an employee's error.
answer: Positive face: the want to be liked, approved of and included.
Negative face: the want to be unimpeded and free from imposition.
Public correction threatens positive face — it damages the employee's standing in front of others.
Mitigation might include praise first, hedging, or correcting in private instead.

card.title: Politeness, face and face-threatening acts
card.front: Brown and Levinson’s politeness theory — the whole model.
back: Face = public self-image that everyone wants respected
Positive face — the want to be liked, approved of, included
Negative face — the want to be unimpeded and not imposed upon
A face-threatening act (FTA) damages one or the other
Positive politeness — compliments, in-group language, agreement
Negative politeness — hedging, apology, indirectness, modals
More social distance or power difference → more mitigation

points.title: Overt and covert prestige
points.detail: Prestige attached to standard variants used by powerful groups, versus prestige attached to local forms that mark solidarity.

questions.q: Explain why covert prestige can lead a speaker to retain a stigmatised feature despite social pressure to drop it.
answer: Covert prestige is the value a non-standard form carries within a group.
Retaining it signals authenticity, loyalty and membership of that group.
Dropping it may be read as distancing yourself from your community.
The speaker weighs institutional advantage against group belonging — often keeping both varieties in their repertoire.

points.title: Dialect, sociolect and idiolect
points.detail: Variation by geography, by social group, and the unique pattern of an individual at a point in their life.

questions.q: Distinguish between a dialect, a sociolect and an idiolect, giving an example of the kind of variation each describes.
answer: Dialect — variation by geography, e.g. 'potato cake' versus 'scallop' across Australian states.
Sociolect — variation by social group, e.g. the lexis shared by medical professionals or by a teenage friendship group.
Idiolect — one individual's unique combination of features at a point in their life.
All three are systematic varieties, not deviations from a correct standard.

card.title: Dialect, sociolect and idiolect
card.front: Three kinds of variation — distinguish them.
back: Dialect — variation by geography
Sociolect — variation by social group: age, class, occupation, interest
Idiolect — one individual’s unique pattern at a point in their life
All three sit within the same language, not below it
Everyone has an idiolect and belongs to multiple sociolects at once

points.title: Broad, General and Cultivated accents
points.detail: The three accent groups within SAE, and the regional, age and social differences they track.

questions.q: Explain how the three Australian accent groups relate to each other, and why the distinction is a continuum rather than three categories.
answer: Broad, General and Cultivated differ mainly in the realisation of vowels and diphthongs.
Broad has the most distinctly Australian realisations; Cultivated the closest to RP.
Speakers sit at points along a continuous scale, not in discrete boxes.
An individual may also shift along the continuum depending on context and audience.

points.title: Aboriginal Australian Englishes
points.detail: A continuum from close to SAE through to something nearer a creole, with features drawn from non-standard Englishes, contact and colonial language, and First Nations languages.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by Aboriginal Australian Englishes, describe where their features originate, and explain why describing them as 'incorrect English' is inaccurate.
answer: A continuum of varieties ranging from close to Standard Australian English through to near-creole forms.
Features draw on non-standard Englishes, contact and colonial language, and First Nations languages.
They are rule-governed and systematic across all subsystems, with their own consistent patterns.
Calling them incorrect applies SAE norms to a different variety — a prescriptivist judgement, and they carry strong covert prestige and identity function.

card.title: Aboriginal Australian Englishes
card.front: What are they, and what features mark them?
back: A continuum — from close to SAE through to near-creole varieties
Draw on non-standard English, contact and colonial language, First Nations languages
Features across all subsystems: phonology, lexis, syntax, discourse
Legitimate varieties with their own systematic rules, not deficient English
Carry strong covert prestige and mark identity and belonging

points.title: Migrant ethnolects
points.detail: Varieties combining features of Australian English with features of a speaker's first language, functioning as markers of social identity.

questions.q: Define a migrant ethnolect and explain why speakers may use one even when they do not speak the associated heritage language.
answer: A variety combining features of Australian English with features of a community's first language.
Features can appear in phonology, lexis, syntax or discourse.
Later-generation speakers use it as a marker of social and cultural identity and group belonging.
It signals in-group membership rather than linguistic ability in the heritage language.

card.title: Migrant ethnolects
card.front: What is an ethnolect and what does it do?
back: Combines features of Australian English with a speaker’s first language
Features may appear in phonology, lexis, syntax or discourse
Used by later generations who may not speak the original language
Functions as a marker of social and cultural identity
Often stigmatised by outsiders while carrying covert prestige inside the group

points.title: Code switching
points.detail: Moving between languages or varieties within a single interaction as a normal feature of multilingual conversation, and as a marker of belonging.

questions.q: Define code switching and distinguish it from register shifting.
answer: Code switching: moving between languages or distinct varieties within a single interaction.
Register shifting: moving between levels of formality within the same variety.
Code switching often signals group membership, identity or inclusion of a particular listener.
Both are strategic uses of a repertoire, but switching crosses varieties while shifting does not.

points.title: Pidgin, creole and lingua franca
points.detail: A pidgin as nobody's first language, a creole as a pidgin that has become one, and a lingua franca as a shared language between groups.

questions.q: Distinguish between a pidgin, a creole and a lingua franca.
answer: A pidgin is a simplified contact variety that has no native speakers.
A creole is a pidgin that has acquired native speakers and developed full grammatical complexity.
A lingua franca is any shared language used between groups who do not share a first language.
The pidgin/creole distinction rests on native speakers, not on how simple the variety appears.

card.title: Pidgin, creole and lingua franca
card.front: Distinguish the three — this is a standard trap.
back: Pidgin — a simplified contact variety that is nobody’s first language
Creole — a pidgin that has acquired native speakers and full complexity
Lingua franca — any shared language used between different groups
English functions as a global lingua franca
The pidgin/creole line is about native speakers, not about complexity

points.title: Language maintenance, shift and reclamation
points.detail: Resisting an encroaching language, switching to it, and the work of revitalising a language at risk of loss — with particular reference to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages.

questions.q: Distinguish between language maintenance, language shift and language reclamation, and identify which applies to efforts to revive an Aboriginal language with no remaining first-language speakers.
answer: Maintenance: a community continues using its language despite pressure from a dominant one.
Shift: the community progressively moves to the dominant language, often across generations.
Reclamation: reviving a language that has been lost or is at serious risk.
Reviving a language with no remaining first-language speakers is reclamation.

card.title: Language maintenance, shift and reclamation
card.front: Three outcomes when languages come into contact.
back: Maintenance — a community resists an encroaching language
Shift — the community moves to the dominant language, often across generations
Reclamation — reviving a language that has been lost or is at risk
Particularly relevant to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages
Losing a language means losing the knowledge encoded in it

points.title: Slang, colloquial language, jargon and taboo
points.detail: The distinctions between them, since they are routinely confused, and swearing as a separate category again.

questions.q: Distinguish slang from colloquial language and from jargon, and explain why swearing is treated separately.
answer: Colloquial language is informal everyday language, widely understood across the speech community.
Slang is informal, group-specific and changes faster; it marks membership of a particular group.
Jargon is the specialised vocabulary of a field — precise for insiders, exclusionary for outsiders.
Swearing is a separate category because it can build solidarity and express emotion, not only cause offence.

card.title: Slang, colloquial, jargon and taboo
card.front: Four categories that get confused — define each.
back: Colloquial — informal everyday language, widely understood
Slang — informal, group-specific, faster-changing, marks membership
Jargon — specialised terms of a field; precision inside, exclusion outside
Taboo — language a community treats as forbidden
Swearing is its own category and can express solidarity, not only offence

points.title: Social distance and rapport
points.detail: The conceptual space between individuals or groups constructed by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status and occupation — and rapport as agreement or sympathy between them.

questions.q: Explain what constructs social distance between participants, and describe two linguistic choices a speaker might make to reduce it.
answer: Social distance is constructed by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status and occupation.
Choice: shifting to colloquial lexis, slang or hypocoristics to signal shared identity.
Choice: positive politeness — first names, inclusive 'we', agreement, in-group markers.
Reducing distance builds rapport; widening it asserts authority.

card.title: Social distance and rapport
card.front: What constructs social distance, and what is rapport?
back: Social distance — the conceptual space between participants
Built by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status, occupation
Greater distance → more formality, more negative politeness
Rapport — agreement, sympathy and ease between participants
Speakers actively reduce distance to build rapport, or widen it to assert authority

points.title: Multi-word lexemes and context-specific graphemes
points.detail: Sequences stored and retrieved as one unit, such as idioms and phrasal verbs; and written symbols whose meaning depends entirely on context.

questions.q: Define a multi-word lexeme and give two examples of different types.
answer: A sequence of words stored and retrieved as a single unit of meaning.
Idiom: 'kick the bucket' — meaning is not derivable from the individual words.
Phrasal verb: 'put up with'.
Also acceptable: compound nouns, fixed collocations.

card.title: Emojis, graphemes and multi-word lexemes
card.front: How do written informal texts replace prosody, and what is a multi-word lexeme?
back: Emojis and emoticons substitute for facial expression and tone
Meaning is context-specific and shifts between groups and generations
Capitals, repeated letters and punctuation stand in for volume and pitch
Context-specific graphemes — symbols meaningful only in their setting
Multi-word lexeme — stored and retrieved as one unit (idioms, phrasal verbs)
